issues.legal_issue: An omission or variation in a trial court’s local inspection does not by itself invalidate the prosecution case when the inspection is used to appreciate evidence already recorded and the variation is not shown to affect the relevant finding.
material_facts: At the accused’s request, the trial court inspected the scene and conducted a test firing with a single-barrel muzzle-loaded gun rather than the double-barrel gun alleged to have been used in the offence.
The guns were of the same general category, and there was no expert evidence that their firing ranges differed.
The inspection was conducted to assess whether the deceased’s position was within firing range.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in treating the use of a different but similar-category gun during the inspection as a material defect; the omission did not invalidate the prosecution case.
issues.legal_principle: Section 310 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides for local inspection to assist the court in properly appreciating evidence already recorded. The inspection memorandum must be considered with that evidence, and an omission or variation in it does not by itself constitute a material irregularity that vitiates the prosecution case.

rule.if: local_inspection_in_a_criminal_trial and inspection_used_to_appreciate_recorded_evidence and similar_category_test_firearm and not evidence_of_materially_different_firing_range

predicates.local_inspection_in_a_criminal_trial: The court conducting a criminal trial carried out a local inspection.
predicates.inspection_used_to_appreciate_recorded_e: The inspection was intended to help the court appreciate evidence already recorded in the proceeding.
predicates.similar_category_test_firearm: The court used a test firearm in the same general category as the firearm alleged to have been used.
predicates.evidence_of_materially_different_firing_: Evidence established that the test firearm had a materially different firing range from the alleged firearm.

issues.definition: When a criminal trial court uses a local inspection to assess recorded evidence, using a test firearm of a similar category does not invalidate the prosecution case if no evidence establishes a materially different firing range.

issues.legal_issue: A report signed by a government scientific expert may be used as evidence under the general rule for such reports even if its author is not among the officers whose documents may be accepted without examination.
material_facts: The forensic laboratory report was signed by a junior scientific officer in the Ballistics section of a government forensic science laboratory.
The report concerned an item submitted for examination in the criminal proceeding.
The High Court rejected the report because the officer was not among the officers enumerated in the provision permitting certain documents to be accepted without examining their authors.
issues.conclusion: The report could be used as evidence under the general provision governing reports made under the hand of a government scientific expert; the author’s absence from the enumerated list did not make it inadmissible.
issues.legal_principle: Section 293(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure permits a document purporting to be a report under the hand of a government scientific expert on an item submitted for examination in a proceeding to be used as evidence. Section 293(4) identifies officers whose documents the court may accept as valid evidence without examining the author; it does not displace the general provision in subsection (1).

predicates.criminal_proceeding: The report was tendered in an inquiry, trial, or other criminal proceeding.
predicates.report_submitted_for_scientific_examinat: An item or matter was duly submitted to the author for examination or analysis in the proceeding.
predicates.report_signed_by_government_scientific_e: The report was made under the hand of a government scientific expert.

issues.definition: In a criminal proceeding, a report made by a government scientific expert on an item duly submitted for examination may be used as evidence without examining its author.

issues.legal_issue: The prosecution is not required to send pellets recovered from a deceased person’s body for ballistic comparison with the alleged firearm.
material_facts: Two pellets were recovered from the deceased’s lungs during the post-mortem examination and handed to the police.
The pellets were not sent to a ballistic expert to determine whether they had been fired from the recovered gun.
The post-mortem evidence established that the deceased had died from firearm injuries.
issues.conclusion: The failure to send the recovered pellets for ballistic examination did not justify an adverse inference against the prosecution; sending them for comparison was not a legal requirement.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the law does not require pellets recovered from a body to be sent to a ballistic expert to determine whether they were fired from an exhibited firearm. In the circumstances, the recovery of the pellets supported the finding that the death resulted from gunshot injuries.

predicates.firearm_death_case: The prosecution alleges that the deceased died from firearm injuries.
predicates.pellets_recovered_from_body: Pellets were recovered from the deceased’s body.
predicates.pellets_not_sent_for_ballistic_compariso: The recovered pellets were not sent to an expert to compare them with the alleged firearm.

issues.definition: In a case alleging death from firearm injuries, failure to send recovered pellets for comparison does not undermine the prosecution case.

issues.legal_issue: An injury that eyewitnesses did not specifically explain does not discredit the prosecution case when the medical evidence and circumstances support a natural reaction that could have caused it.
material_facts: The medical witness stated that one injury could have been caused if the deceased raised his arm while walking.
The eyewitnesses said that the accused challenged the deceased and then fired, but did not specifically describe the deceased raising his arm.
The Court considered it natural that the deceased might raise his hands in reaction to the challenge or to defend himself.
issues.conclusion: The absence of a specific explanation from the eyewitnesses for the injury did not discredit the prosecution case.
issues.legal_principle: Human reactions are unpredictable and need not follow a fixed pattern. A possible reaction may be assessed in the context of the circumstances and the medical evidence; the Court relied on no specific statutory provision or earlier case for this proposition.

predicates.criminal_trial_evidence: The issue arises in the assessment of evidence in a criminal trial.
predicates.medical_evidence_links_injury_to_possibl: Medical evidence indicates that the injury could have resulted from a particular bodily reaction.
predicates.challenge_or_threat_preceded_injury: A challenge or threat immediately preceded the injury.
predicates.eyewitnesses_did_not_describe_that_react: The eyewitnesses did not specifically state that the injured person made the reaction identified by the medical evidence.

issues.definition: When a challenge or threat precedes an injury and medical evidence links it to a possible reaction, the eyewitnesses’ failure to describe that reaction does not discredit the prosecution case.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of pellet injuries on eyewitnesses does not make their presence at the scene doubtful when the deceased was ahead of them and the shot was directed at the deceased.
material_facts: Two eyewitnesses said that they were accompanying the deceased and that he was walking ahead of them.
The accused challenged the deceased and fired at him.
Pellets had scattered and struck a tree, but the eyewitnesses sustained no pellet injuries.
issues.conclusion: The absence of pellet injuries on the eyewitnesses was not a ground to doubt their presence at the scene.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the absence of injuries in the circumstances, including that the deceased was ahead of the eyewitnesses and was the target of the shot. It relied on no specific statutory provision or earlier case for this conclusion.

rule.if: firearm_attack_case and eyewitnesses_accompanied_victim and victim_was_ahead_of_eyewitnesses and shot_directed_at_victim and eyewitnesses_uninjured

predicates.firearm_attack_case: The prosecution alleges that the accused attacked the victim with a firearm.
predicates.eyewitnesses_accompanied_victim: The eyewitnesses were accompanying the victim at the time of the incident.
predicates.victim_was_ahead_of_eyewitnesses: The victim was walking ahead of the eyewitnesses when the shot was fired.
predicates.shot_directed_at_victim: The firearm was aimed or directed at the victim.
predicates.eyewitnesses_uninjured: The eyewitnesses sustained no injuries from the shot or its pellets.

issues.definition: When eyewitnesses accompany a victim who is ahead of them and the shot is directed at the victim, their lack of injuries does not make their presence doubtful.

issues.legal_issue: Relationship to the deceased or an alleged motive to support the prosecution does not by itself justify rejecting eyewitness testimony that inspires confidence after cautious assessment.
material_facts: Two eyewitnesses were relatives of the deceased, and one was also related to a person with whom the accused had a civil dispute.
The witnesses gave categorical accounts of the shooting and were subjected to lengthy cross-examination, which did not elicit anything that undermined their creditworthiness.

Their presence with the deceased was natural in the circumstances, and another witness who was independent of both sides also gave evidence about seeing the accused with a gun and fleeing after the shot.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in rejecting the related eyewitnesses at the threshold because of their relationship and alleged interest; their testimony had to be assessed with caution and could be relied upon because it inspired confidence.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the settled principle that a witness’s relationship to a party is not, by itself, a ground for disbelieving the witness. The testimony must instead be examined with caution to determine whether it inspires confidence. No earlier case was named in the judgment.

rule.if: criminal_trial_testimony and eyewitness_related_to_deceased and testimony_survives_cross_examination and testimony_inspires_confidence

predicates.criminal_trial_testimony: The evidence is testimony given by an eyewitness in a criminal trial.
predicates.eyewitness_related_to_deceased: The eyewitness is related to the deceased or has a relationship that may create an interest in the prosecution outcome.
predicates.testimony_survives_cross_examination: Cross-examination does not elicit material that undermines the eyewitness’s creditworthiness.
predicates.testimony_inspires_confidence: After cautious assessment, the eyewitness’s testimony is found credible.

issues.definition: Related eyewitness testimony that survives cross-examination and inspires confidence after cautious assessment is not rejected solely because of the witness’s relationship or interest.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court must not set aside a trial conviction on unsupported or perverse evidentiary grounds while disregarding consistent eyewitness evidence corroborated by medical and forensic evidence.
material_facts: The trial court convicted the accused after finding the prosecution case proved beyond reasonable doubt.
Three witnesses gave consistent evidence implicating the accused, and their accounts were corroborated by the post-mortem evidence and the forensic laboratory report.

The High Court set aside the conviction on grounds concerning the local inspection, the scientific report, the unsent pellets, an injury, the eyewitnesses’ lack of injuries, and the witnesses’ relationships.
The Supreme Court found those grounds fallacious or perverse and held that the High Court had not properly considered the eyewitness evidence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s order was set aside, the trial court’s conviction and sentence were restored, and the prosecution appeal was allowed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held, on its assessment of the evidence, that the consistent eyewitness accounts corroborated by medical and forensic evidence established the prosecution case beyond reasonable doubt, and that the High Court’s failure to consider that evidence while relying on fallacious grounds resulted in a grave error. The judgment cites no specific provision or earlier case for this overall appellate conclusion.

rule.if: prosecution_appeal_from_high_court_acquittal and trial_conviction_based_on_proof_beyond_reasonable_doubt and consistent_eyewitness_accounts and medical_and_forensic_corroboration and high_court_relied_on_unsupported_or_perverse_grounds

predicates.prosecution_appeal_from_high_court_acqui: The prosecution appeals after a High Court has set aside a trial conviction and acquitted the accused.
predicates.trial_conviction_based_on_proof_beyond_r: The trial court convicted the accused after finding the prosecution case proved beyond reasonable doubt.
predicates.consistent_eyewitness_accounts: The eyewitnesses gave consistent accounts implicating the accused.
predicates.medical_and_forensic_corroboration: Medical and forensic evidence corroborated the eyewitness accounts.
predicates.high_court_relied_on_unsupported_or_perv: The High Court set aside the conviction on grounds that were unsupported by evidence or were perverse.

issues.definition: When a prosecution appeal follows a High Court acquittal, the trial conviction rested on proof beyond reasonable doubt, eyewitness accounts are consistent and medically and forensically corroborated, and the High Court relied on unsupported or perverse grounds, the trial conviction is restored.
